objectives: Group the major .NET numeric types by the kind of problem they solve instead of memorizing a list.
Explain why the same visible value can have different internal numeric representations.
Predict why 0.1 + 0.2 differs between double and decimal arithmetic.
Choose int, long, double, or decimal for common beginner scenarios.
Describe precision, range, memory, and performance as tradeoffs rather than a search for one best numeric type.

visuals.title: Start with purpose, not a type table
visuals.explanation: The family becomes manageable when grouped into whole numbers, approximate measurements, and base-10 business values. Most programs repeatedly use only a few defaults.

visuals.title: Appearance is not representation
visuals.explanation: Both double and decimal can display 100.99. Their difference is how they model the value internally and which arithmetic they are designed to perform.

visuals.title: Some fractions fit one system better
visuals.explanation: Decimal tenths fit decimal arithmetic directly. Binary floating-point often stores the nearest available value, which is excellent for measurements but can expose a tiny difference.

visuals.title: Every choice balances tradeoffs
visuals.explanation: A type offers a combination of precision, range, memory use, and calculation speed. Choose the combination that matches the meaning of the value.

preQuiz.prompt: Which type is the normal first choice for a whole-number count such as 42 employees?
preQuiz.explanation: Use int for most ordinary whole numbers unless the domain gives you a reason to choose differently.

preQuiz.prompt: Can both double and decimal store a value written as 100.99?
options: No, only decimal can contain a decimal point
Yes, but they represent and calculate with that value differently
Yes, and they are interchangeable in every expression
preQuiz.explanation: The visible business value can be the same while the internal representation and arithmetic model differ.

preQuiz.prompt: Which type usually best communicates a product price?
preQuiz.explanation: Prices are base-10 business values, so decimal usually matches their meaning and expected arithmetic.

concept.title: Why does .NET have so many numeric types?
paragraphs: Different numbers do different jobs. An employee count is a whole number. A distance from a sensor is a measurement. A product price follows base-10 business rules.

No single representation gives the widest range, most useful precision, smallest memory use, and fastest calculations for every job. The numeric family lets code state which tradeoffs and meaning matter.

concept.title: A practical map of the integer family
paragraphs: Integer types store whole numbers. Do not begin by memorizing their limits. Begin with int, the normal default for ordinary counts, indexes, ages, and quantities.

Use long when a count can become much larger than int is intended to handle. The remaining integer types are specialized choices you will recognize when an API or a carefully constrained domain calls for them.

list.text: byte, sbyte, short, and ushort. Useful when a deliberately small value or an existing data format requires one; uncommon as everyday defaults.
int and uint. int is the usual choice. uint represents non-negative whole numbers but is less convenient in ordinary application code, so non-negative meaning alone does not make it the default.
long and ulong. long is the practical choice for very large counts. ulong is a specialized non-negative alternative.

closingParagraphs: The u in uint, ushort, and ulong means unsigned: the type does not represent negative values. sbyte is the explicitly signed partner of byte. You only need to recognize that distinction here, not memorize limits.

concept.title: float and double model approximate measurements
paragraphs: float and double are binary floating-point types. Think of them as scientific calculators that cover a very wide span of values and efficiently handle measurements, coordinates, graphics, engineering, and scientific calculations.

They use a binary number system internally. Some simple-looking base-10 fractions do not fit that system exactly, so the stored value is the closest available approximation. double is the normal default; float is mainly chosen when an API or a large graphics or measurement workload specifically benefits from it.

concept.title: decimal models base-10 business arithmetic
paragraphs: decimal is designed for values whose decimal digits carry business meaning: money, prices, tax rates, account balances, and similar base-10 quantities.

It can store values such as 0.1 and 0.2 directly in decimal form, so familiar base-10 calculations behave as expected. It still has finite precision; its advantage is alignment with decimal arithmetic, not infinite accuracy.

concept.title: The same visible value can use two representations
paragraphs: Both declarations below describe the business value one hundred dollars and ninety-nine cents. They may print the same text. The difference is below the surface.

The double value uses binary floating-point and is well suited to approximate measurement calculations. The decimal value uses decimal arithmetic and is well suited to a price. How a value looks on screen does not tell you how it is represented.

concept.title: Why 0.1 + 0.2 exposes the difference
paragraphs: In binary floating-point, 0.1 and 0.2 are stored as very close approximations because those decimal fractions do not fit neatly in the binary system. Adding the approximations can produce a result just beside exact 0.3, so a direct equality check can be false.

In decimal arithmetic, 0.1m and 0.2m are represented as decimal tenths. Their sum is 0.3m, so the equality check is true. This does not make double broken; it means double and decimal are designed for different kinds of calculation.

concept.title: Why decimal literals use the m suffix
paragraphs: A numeric literal with a decimal point is treated as double by default. Writing 100.99m tells the compiler to create a decimal literal from the beginning.

The suffix makes the choice visible and prevents an unnoticed change from binary floating-point into decimal arithmetic. Think of m as the marker for a decimal money-style value; it is part of the literal, not part of the variable name.

concept.title: Use four questions instead of memorizing every type
paragraphs: Precision asks how finely and predictably the value must be represented. Range asks how small or large it may become. Memory asks how much space matters when many values are stored. Performance asks how often and how quickly calculations must run.

For ordinary application code, meaning comes first. Use int for most whole numbers, long for very large counts, double for scientific, engineering, graphics, and measurement work, and decimal for money and other base-10 business values.
Smaller integer types and float remain useful, but choose them when a real requirement, data format, or API gives you a reason—not because they appear more economical in isolation.

postQuiz.prompt: Why can double price = 100.99 and decimal price = 100.99m print the same value but behave differently in later calculations?
options: decimal automatically rounds every value to two places
postQuiz.explanation: Visible text can match even though binary floating-point and decimal arithmetic represent and calculate with the value differently.

postQuiz.prompt: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 commonly false for double?
options: Those decimal fractions are stored as nearby binary approximations
postQuiz.explanation: The addition combines nearby binary approximations, and the result can sit just beside exact decimal 0.3.

postQuiz.prompt: Which pairing best follows the lesson's practical defaults?
options: int for ordinary counts; decimal for prices
byte for every count; double for money
decimal for graphics; ulong for temperatures
postQuiz.explanation: int is the normal whole-number default, while decimal communicates base-10 business arithmetic.

postQuiz.prompt: What does the m in 100.99m do?
options: Makes the literal decimal instead of the default double
Stores the value in memory immediately
postQuiz.explanation: The suffix tells the compiler that the literal itself has type decimal.

reflections: Why is 'Does this value have a decimal point?' not enough information to choose between double and decimal?
Which matters more for a product price: a wide measurement range or familiar base-10 arithmetic?
When might a specialized type such as byte, uint, or float be justified instead of the usual default?
whatBreaks: Removing the comparison leaves students with syntax but no reason for choosing a numeric type. They may use decimal for every fractional value, use double for financial calculations because it prints correctly, or select small integer types without a requirement. The program may compile while its arithmetic communicates the wrong domain intent.
summary: .NET has multiple numeric types because whole-number counts, approximate measurements, and base-10 business values need different tradeoffs. Start with int for ordinary whole numbers, long for very large counts, double for measurements and scientific or graphics work, and decimal for money and base-10 business arithmetic. The same visible value can use different internal representations; the m suffix makes a decimal literal explicit.
